Metrics, traces and request ids for every egradx library and application, for Node. It is the counterpart of the Java `egradx-observability` (docs/observability/guide.md) and depends on no other egradx package.

It is written against the OpenTelemetry API only. It records nothing until the application registers an OpenTelemetry SDK, just as Java records nothing without Actuator:

| The application has | It gets |
|---|---|
| Nothing extra | Every observation and metric call costs nothing. `send` still gives stored work a request id. |
| A `MeterProvider` (`@opentelemetry/sdk-metrics`, e.g. with a Prometheus exporter) | Timers (unit `s`) and counters for everything egradx instruments. |
| A `TracerProvider`, a context manager and the W3C propagator (`NodeTracerProvider.register()` from `@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-node` sets all three; `@opentelemetry/sdk-node` does too, but also exports logs and traces from `OTEL_*` defaults) | Spans. Work handed off through a database outbox stays in the trace of the request that caused it. |

| Export | What it is |
|---|---|
| `EgradxObservations` | Java's `EgradxObservations`. `observe(module, operation, body)` gives a timer `egradx.<module>.<operation>` and a span `"<module> <operation>"`, both carrying `egradx.outcome`: `success`, or `error` if the body throws (or rejects) without having set another. `send` / `receive` carry a trace through stored work; `consumer` starts an observation that is stopped elsewhere, as the notification dispatcher's are. `noop()` records nothing. |
| `EgradxTraceContext` | What is stored with work handed off: the propagator's `traceparent` (and `tracestate`), plus the `requestId`. `serialize()` / `parse()` write and read the same text as Java (`contracts/test-vectors/observability.json`); `parse` never throws. |
| `otelMetrics(meterProvider?)`, `noopMetrics`, `EgradxMetrics` | Counters, gauges and timers for what has no span. `record` takes milliseconds and stores seconds. |
| `TIMER_BUCKETS` | The bucket boundaries of every timer, in seconds (5 ms to 10 s), OpenTelemetry's for HTTP durations; the SDK's defaults are for milliseconds. |
| `EgradxTagRules` | Java's rules, with its messages: names start with `egradx.`; no tag key naming an id, address, URL or path; no value that looks like a UUID or is longer than 64 characters. Checked even when nothing is recorded, so a bad tag fails a test. |
| `withMdc`, `mdcValue`, `mdcValues`, `MDC_*` | Java's MDC: values for log lines, carried across `await` by `AsyncLocalStorage`. |
| `correlationFields()`, `correlationPrefix()`, `currentTraceId()` | The MDC values plus the active span's `traceId` and `spanId`; the prefix is Java's `[traceId,spanId,requestId] `; the trace id alone is for an error body, as Java's `EgradxRequestContext.currentTraceId()`. |
| `egradxPinoOptions()`, `egradxPinoMixin()` | The same fields on every pino log line. pino is an optional peer dependency and is never imported. |

```ts
const observations = new EgradxObservations();   // the global OpenTelemetry providers
return observations.observe('auth', 'login', (observation) => {
  observation.tag(EgradxObservations.OUTCOME, 'auth_invalid_credentials');   // timer + span
  observation.detail('egradx.user.id', userId);                              // span only
  return result;
});
```

## Log shipping

`EgradxLogShipper` sends log lines on, as Java's `EgradxLogShippingAppender`:
- each line carries its trace, request, person and organization (`userId` and `organizationId` are put in the logging context by `@babulvaibhav/egradx-express`'s `authenticate`);
- logging only queues the line, in a bounded queue (10 000 by default);
- one sender sends batches of 200 at most every second;
- when the queue is full, lines are dropped and counted (`dropped()`).

`egradxShippingDestination(shipper)` is a pino destination for `pino.multistream`. Any other logger can call `shipper.offer(...)`. The sink is `@babulvaibhav/egradx-events`' `events.logSink`, which sends `egradx.log.record.v1` events.

## Tests

- **The contract vector:** the trace context written and read as Java does, and Java's names and tag messages.
- **Log shipping:** in `@babulvaibhav/egradx-events`' suite, where the shipped lines arrive as events.
- **Against the OpenTelemetry SDK** with in-memory exporters: the timer and span of an observation, outcomes on failure, a trace carried from `send` to `receive` (the receiving span a child of the sending one, with the request id in the MDC), a consumer stopped twice, the noop instance, metrics, and pino log lines carrying the ids.

## Classes

### EgradxLogShipper

Ships the application's log lines to an EgradxLogSink, with the trace, request, person and organization each was
logged for, as Java's EgradxLogShippingAppender. Best effort: logging only adds the line to a bounded queue; a timer
sends batches, one at a time; when the queue is full, lines are dropped and counted, so shipping can never slow the
application or fill its memory.

  const shipper = new EgradxLogShipper(events.logSink(), { service: 'orders' });
  const log = pino({ ...egradxPinoOptions() }, pino.multistream([{ stream: process.stdout }, { stream: egradxShippingDestination(shipper) }]));

Any other logger can call `offer` itself.

### EgradxObservations

The one way egradx code times an operation: a timer `egradx.<module>.<operation>` (seconds) when the application has an
OpenTelemetry meter provider, a span "<module> <operation>" when it has a tracer provider, and nothing when it has
neither. Every observation carries `egradx.outcome`: `success` unless the code sets another, `error` if it throws
without having set one, so all samples of one timer have the same tag keys. Work handed to another thread or process
is a send and later a receive: send captures the trace into an EgradxTraceContext to store with the work; receive
and consumer continue it where the work is picked up. As Java's EgradxObservations.

### EgradxTraceContext

Where a piece of work came from, in a form that can be written into a database row or a message and picked up again
later: what a tracer's propagator writes (the W3C traceparent, and tracestate or baggage if any), plus the requestId of
the HTTP request that started it. Without a tracer only the request id is there, which is still enough to find every
log line and row a request produced. Immutable; never throws on bad input. As Java's EgradxTraceContext, whose text
every SDK writes and reads alike (contracts/test-vectors/observability.json).

`egradx.log.record.v1` event's data (contracts/events/schemas/egradx.log.record.v1.json), as Java's EgradxLogRecord.

### EgradxMetrics

Counters, gauges and timers for what has no natural span: messages given up on, the size of a backlog, open
connections. Timed operations should use EgradxObservations instead, which gives a timer and a span from one call.
Names start with `egradx.`; tags are alternating key, value pairs, checked by EgradxTagRules even when metrics are off,
so a bad tag fails a test. As Java's EgradxMetrics.

## Variables

### EgradxTagRules

```ts
const EgradxTagRules: object;
```

What may be a metric name or a metric tag, checked on every call so that a mistake fails a test instead of taking down a
metrics backend. As Java's EgradxTagRules, with its messages.

Every distinct combination of tag values is a separate time series. A tag whose values are unbounded (an organization
id, a user id, a request id) grows that set without limit, and ids and addresses are personal data besides. They
belong on spans, never on meters. So names start with `egradx.`, tag keys that name an id, an address, a URL or a path
are refused, and values that look like a UUID or are longer than 64 characters are refused.

#### Type Declaration

| Name | Type | Default value | Description |
| ------ | ------ | ------ | ------ |
| <a id="property-max_value_length"></a> `MAX_VALUE_LENGTH` | `number` | `64` | - |
| <a id="property-prefix"></a> `PREFIX` | `string` | `'egradx.'` | - |
| `checkName()` | (`name`) => `string` | - | A meter or observation name: `egradx.` then dot-separated lower-case words. |
| `checkSegment()` | (`segment`) => `string` | - | One module or operation segment of a name, such as `notification` or `bulk.expansion`. |
| `checkTag()` | (`key`, `value`) => `void` | - | - |
| `checkTags()` | (`keyValues`) => `Record`\<`string`, `string`\> | - | Checks alternating key, value pairs and returns them as attributes. |

### noopMetrics

```ts
const noopMetrics: EgradxMetrics;
```

Records nothing, but checks every name and tag.

***

### TIMER\_BUCKETS

```ts
const TIMER_BUCKETS: number[];
```

The bucket boundaries of every egradx timer, in seconds: OpenTelemetry's for HTTP durations. The SDK's defaults (0, 5,
10, 25…) are made for milliseconds and would put every operation in the first bucket.

## Functions

### correlationFields()

```ts
function correlationFields(): Record<string, string>;
```

What a log line of the current work should carry, as Java's MDC gives logback: the logging context's values (requestId,
and whatever else the work put there, such as a delivery's deliveryId) and, with a tracer, the active span's traceId
and spanId. Empty outside any request or traced work.

#### Returns

`Record`\<`string`, `string`\>

***

### correlationPrefix()

```ts
function correlationPrefix(): string;
```

The correlation part of a log line, as Java's `logging.pattern.correlation` writes it:
`[traceId,spanId,requestId] `, each empty when absent. For loggers that write plain text.

#### Returns

`string`

***

### currentTraceId()

```ts
function currentTraceId(): string | undefined;
```

The trace id of the current work, for an error body, as Java's `EgradxRequestContext.currentTraceId()`; undefined
without a tracer.

#### Returns

`string` \| `undefined`

***

### egradxPinoMixin()

```ts
function egradxPinoMixin(): () => Record<string, string>;
```

pino's `mixin`: every log line gets the correlation fields.

  const log = pino({ ...egradxPinoOptions() });

#### Returns

() => `Record`\<`string`, `string`\>

***

```ts
function egradxPinoOptions(): object;
```

The pino options that make its log lines carry the correlation fields; spread them into your own.

`object`

| Name | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `mixin()` | () => `Record`\<`string`, `string`\> |

***

### egradxShippingDestination()

```ts
function egradxShippingDestination(shipper, options?): object;
```

A pino destination that ships each line pino writes, besides wherever else the application sends them (use it in
`pino.multistream`). Lines carry their correlation fields when the logger has egradxPinoOptions' mixin; otherwise
the current work's are taken, as pino writes in the logging call's own context.

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `shipper` | [`EgradxLogShipper`](#egradxlogshipper) |
| `options` | \{ `logger?`: `string`; \} |
| `options.logger?` | `string` |

#### Returns

`object`

| Name | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `write()` | (`line`) => `void` |

### withMdc()

```ts
function withMdc<T>(values, fn): T;
```

Runs `fn` with these values added to the logging context, as Java's EgradxMdcScope: null and undefined values are
skipped; the values before are back once `fn` (and anything it awaits) is done.

#### Type Parameters

| Type Parameter |
| ------ |
| `T` |

#### Parameters

| Parameter | Type |
| ------ | ------ |
| `values` | `Record`\<`string`, `string` \| `null` \| `undefined`\> |
| `fn` | () => `T` |

#### Returns

`T`
